clue.text: The lower island ?

parts.note: a 'lower' here is one that lows, a cow, so the island is the one that gave its name to a famous breed of dairy cattle

explanation.surface: A question about which island lies further down or to the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' reads as 'further down' but is lower as in a cow lowing: the Channel Island of Jersey gives its name to a dairy breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey is a Channel Island and also a breed of cattle, the mooing creatures the clue calls lowers.

clue.text: Letters written to one demanding resin

parts.note: the letters L and M written out in full as words are 'el' and 'em'
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone writes letters to a person who is insisting on being sent resin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters written' means two letters spelt as words, EL and EM; 'to one' adds I, the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is a fragrant gum resin from tropical trees, used in varnishes and ointments.

clue.text: Court limits subsidiary activities?

explanation.surface: A tennis court's boundaries double as a person's side projects.
explanation.definitionFit: The lines marking the edges of a sports court are its touchlines; sidelines are also extra jobs held alongside the main one.

clue.text: Submits returns ?

explanation.surface: Someone gives in and hands back what was asked.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give way or surrender; yields are also the profits or harvest an investment or field produces.

clue.text: Part of the ship aft, possibly -easily damaged

indicators.note: possibly says the word aft is only one arrangement of its letters, so they may be shuffled

parts.note: something easily damaged is frail

explanation.surface: Describing a fragile part at the back of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges AFT to TAF, and FRAIL follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The taffrail is the rail round the stern of a ship.

clue.text: Where Mr Darling went for a book?

definitions.text: Where Mr Darling went for a book?

parts.words: Where Mr Darling went for a book?
parts.note: Grace Darling's father William kept the Longstone light off Northumberland, so going to his work and the title of a Virginia Woolf novel are the same phrase

explanation.surface: Asking where a Mr Darling popped out to borrow something to read.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Darling suggests the father in Peter Pan, but it is William Darling, lighthouse-keeper father of the rescuer Grace Darling; the destination is also Virginia Woolf's 1927 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A Woolf novel named after a family's planned trip to a coastal beacon, which is also where a lighthouse-keeper goes to work.

clue.text: Novelist finds another without point

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the other novelist's name goes round the point

parts.note: another novelist, E. M. Forster, author of A Passage to India
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: One writer discovers a rival who is pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'without point' as 'lacking E' and the clue says the same thing: C. S. Forester minus E is Forster. As written, 'without' means outside, putting FORSTER round E.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester wrote the Hornblower naval novels.

clue.text: Show gets a sound critique

indicators.note: sound here means as heard, so a word for the critique is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a critique is a review

explanation.surface: A stage show receives a solid, reasonable write-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like praise for the critique but signals that REVIEW is said aloud, giving REVUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A revue is a theatrical show of sketches, songs and dances.

clue.text: Excites attention when collecting site's rent .

indicators.note: collecting means gathering the letters of site's rent up and putting them together anew

explanation.surface: A landlord gets interested when the rent for the site is collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collecting' rearranges the letters of SITE'S RENT; 'when' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To engage someone's curiosity is to arouse their attention.

clue.text: Law not enforced by late property-owner ?

parts.note: late means dead, as in 'the late Mr Smith'
a property-owner who lets out a house is a letter

explanation.surface: A rule left unenforced by a landowner who has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' is one who lets property, not a written message.
explanation.definitionFit: A law still on the books but no longer applied in practice.

clue.text: Vessels returned are some of the first available

indicators.note: returned means the letters picked out are read backwards
some of means only part of the phrase is used, a run inside the words

explanation.surface: Containers sent back include the first ones that were available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some of' takes STAV from 'firST AVailable'; 'returned' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Vats are large tanks or tubs for holding liquids.

clue.text: Remove Gide's old novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of the French author's name and old are made into something new

explanation.surface: Getting rid of an old novel by André Gide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book by Gide but signals an anagram of GIDES and OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to shift it out of position.

clue.text: Guides the herd

explanation.surface: Someone directs a crowd of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer is to direct a course; steers are young castrated bulls, a herd of cattle.

clue.text: Green material ?

explanation.surface: Asking about fabric of a verdant colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawn is a stretch of mown grass, green; lawn is also a fine linen or cotton fabric.

clue.text: Hate to be in a crowd standing up in the tea break

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a crowd is a mob
taken as written

indicators.note: break means the letters of tea are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone loathes having to stand in a crowd during the tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing up' turns MOB to BOM in this down clue; 'break' rearranges TEA to ATE; 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To abominate is to loathe or detest.

clue.text: Impractical person reveals something about ladies' make-up

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the word for something goes round the reworked letters

parts.note: it stands for an unspecified thing

indicators.note: make-up is read as making the letters up again in a new order

explanation.surface: A dreamer exposes the truth about women's cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make-up' looks like cosmetics but rearranges LADIES to DEALIS; 'about' puts IT round it; 'reveals' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealist pursues perfect standards rather than what is realistic.

clue.text: City transplant stock, perhaps ?

parts.note: a stock of organs kept for transplant surgery could be called a pool of livers, which also names a port city in north-west England

explanation.surface: A city's supply of material ready for transplanting.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as liver + pool: a reserve of livers for transplant.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool is a major English port city on the Mersey, and split up it reads as a pooled supply of organs.

clue.text: Simple barbarian includes bad poems

indicators.note: includes means the barbarian word takes the scrambled letters inside it

parts.note: the Huns were barbarian invaders of the Roman Empire

indicators.note: bad means the poems are badly made, their letters jumbled

explanation.surface: An unsophisticated savage collects some poor verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges POEMS to OMESP, which 'includes' sets inside HUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Homespun means plain and unpretentious, like cloth woven at home.

clue.text: Truly ironical

parts.note: an old word for 'in truth' that survives mainly in mock-serious or sarcastic use

explanation.definitionFit: Forsooth is archaic for 'indeed', now mostly used with scorn or irony.

clue.text: Number going by sea perhaps in this vessel

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five, a number

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of sea may be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Someone sends a numbered container off by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges SEA to ASE after V.
explanation.definitionFit: A vase is a decorative container for flowers.

clue.text: Moroccan port is to free Mohammedan commander-put-up job

parts.note: an aga is a commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means the word is raised, read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to rid is to free

explanation.surface: A Moroccan port releases a Muslim commander in what was a rigged plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put-up job' reads as a rigged scheme; 'put-up' turns RID to DIR in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Agadir is a city and harbour on Morocco's Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Bill comes in to discharge vehicle

indicators.note: comes in means the bill's letters are placed inside the word for discharge

parts.note: to discharge a gun is to fire it
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: An invoice arrives to send away a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discharge' looks like getting rid of the vehicle but means FIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiacre is a small four-wheeled French hackney carriage.

clue.text: Part of a trunk or box ?

explanation.surface: Asking about a section of a travelling case or crate.
explanation.definitionFit: The thorax is the upper part of the body's torso; a chest is also a sturdy lidded storage box.

clue.text: The Pennine Way, perhaps ?

parts.note: the long-distance footpath runs along the hills of northern England, so it is an elevated route, which is also a word for a main road

explanation.definitionFit: A highroad is a main road, and the hill path is literally a route up high.

clue.text: British statesman of the year 1000, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the letters given may be put into another order

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A British politician who belongs to the year 1000.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges YEAR plus M; 'of the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo Amery was a Conservative Cabinet minister of the 1920s to 1940s.

clue.text: Female or male comedian ?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a comic is a woman or a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A dame is a woman of rank; the pantomime dame, in British Christmas shows, is a comic woman's part played by a man.

clue.text: Perhaps they are paid to play badly

definitions.text: Perhaps they are paid to play badly

parts.words: Perhaps they are paid to play badly
parts.note: notes of one denomination are banknotes paid out

explanation.surface: Musicians who are given money for a poor performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper money of a sterling denomination, read as a phrase about hammering a keyboard.

clue.text: Condemn 'in so many words'?

explanation.surface: Damning someone in plain, explicit language.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge passes judgment to punish; a sentence is also a group of words expressing a complete thought.

clue.text: Fresh horses in fifty, years ? .Must be wrong !

indicators.note: the exclamation that the figure must be wrong says the letters given are to be rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty

explanation.surface: Someone doubts that horses could be fresh at fifty years old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must be wrong' rearranges L and YEARS; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Relays are fresh teams of horses set out along a route to replace tired ones.
